questions.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form
questions.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=3v-7u+7,\,y=v-2u+3.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax+by-2,\,v=-2x+7y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3v-7u+7 \\ v-2u+3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7u+3v \\ -2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-7)-3\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-7 \\ y-3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1\cdot (x-7)+3\cdot (y-3) \\ -2\cdot (x-7)+7\cdot (y-3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-x+3y-2 \\ -2x+7y-7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=(-1)x+3y-2,\,v=-2x+7y+(-7).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-1+3+(-7)=-5.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Part of a Sphere in Spherical Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/9f7ed51c1273b73243beb574535686f4ce3498b28c84cbe76833a3096674792c.png)

The solid enclosed by the quarter-sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0$ and $y\le 0,$ shown above, can be described in spherical polar coordinates as
questions.worked_solution:
We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/d338181a6631c513330ef2dd3899cfb9b01cb6f4c4ff7d9cd65038b381e7fec4.png)

  

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary withing the following domains:

- $\rho \in [0,3]$

- $\theta \in [\frac{3\pi }{2},2\pi ]$

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Expressing Part of a Sphere in Spherical Coordinates

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/d1c2f0e830c6d3beca27886e839816f46a00be322c9d7cff18248d118ed0e617.png)

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type I region in two-dimensional space?
questions.worked_solution:
A type I region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le x\le b,\,g(x)\le y\le f(x)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type I region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $x:$

$$
x=\sqrt{3-y}+1\,⟹\,y=3-(x-1)^{2}
$$

The function $y=0$ is already written as a function of $x.$

Notice that the region lies between the vertical lines $x=1$ and $x=2.$ So, we have $0\le x\le 1.$

We draw a vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower function $g(x)$ and the upper function $f(x).$ A vertical line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type I region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/be799df2140d3a437bb311427dcae0e297cb6bd3844f88932157eb6ace6e7e59.png)

The vertical line enters the region through the lower function $y=0$ and leaves through the upper function $y=3-(x-1)^{2}.$ So, we have $0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Center of Mass for a Collection of Masses Along the X-Axis
questions.problem: Consider the collection of point masses ${m}_{1}=4\,\text{kg},$ ${m}_{2}=6\,\text{kg},$ and ${m}_{3}=8\,\text{kg}$ located at ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=-1,$ and ${x}_{3}=3,$ respectively, along the $x$-axis, where the $x$-coordinates are measured in meters. What is the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass for this system?
questions.worked_solution:
The center of mass, denoted $\overset{―}{x},$ of a collection of point masses ${m}_{1},{m}_{2},…,{m}_{n}$ located at ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ along the $x$-axis is given by 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $m={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}$ is the total mass of the system,

- ${M}_{O}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i}$ is the total moment of the system about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =4, & \,{m}_{2} & =6, & \,{m}_{3} & =8, \\ {x}_{1} & =-3, & \,{x}_{2} & =-1, & \,{x}_{3} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total mass of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}+{m}_{2}+{m}_{3} \\  & =4+6+8 \\  & =18\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

and the moment of the system about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}{x}_{1}+{m}_{2}{x}_{2}+{m}_{3}{x}_{3} \\  & =4\cdot (-3)+6\cdot (-1)+8\cdot 3 \\  & =-12-6+24 \\  & =6\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{6}{18}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Center of Mass for a Collection of Masses Along the X-Axis

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Sum and Constant Multiple Rules
questions.worked_solution:
The sum and constant multiple rules for double summations state that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{ij}, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}k{a}_{ij} & =k{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying these rules to the given sum, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}2({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) \\  & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}{a}_{ij}+2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}{b}_{ij} \\  & =2\cdot 75+2\cdot 70 \\  & =150+140 \\  & =290.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Interior of a Set
questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,-1\le y<0}.
$$

The interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<2,\,\,}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/fc71859cb4d1e58ea3d15c2da66bce014898281fe237f2e0c2396f96c84c9e79.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/eff037b96b6a42120fdfa112a98d1e0749cdd56bd89acd647db448b08d7323ad.png)

So, in this case, the interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<2,\,-1<y<0\,}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying the Interior of a Set

questions.knowledge_point: Domains of Functions With Exponential and Logarithmic Components
questions.problem: Find the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=2\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)\,k.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the domain of $f$, we need the intersection of the domains of the individual components.

- The domain of the 1st component $2$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 2nd component ${t}^{2}$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 3rd component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)$ is $t\in (-1,\infty ).$

The intersection is illustrated in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/44e047a975ee3b2ad7966b95bbba3a6270925f451c8cb8c6dac6dbef532f2b7a.png)

Therefore, the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is $t\in (-1,\infty ).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Function Is a Valid PDF
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/8f955ee719a4e69f0d09c678f0a74023f137efd7b5ae36d49b98706156384173.png)

Consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown above.

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x+\frac{1}{2},\, & 0<x<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$
- ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$
- $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{0}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

choices.value: None of the statements are true

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a General Solution in Implicit Form
